rv.q: And, for all the digital and industrial bombast of the new staging, the hero of the evening is Wells’ prose, describing with economical selection of terrible details the ruin of the UK. There is a particular frisson when Neeson describes incinerated bodies piled on Euston Road and the streets of Bloomsbury in London, just outside the theatre.
The director, Bob Tomson, does his best to bring it to life, but struggles to create human drama in a script that’s better imagined than staged.
This is high-end cheese, and at points it's delightfully entertaining as such.
I have sat through some duff shows at the Dominion Theatre but this one takes the cake.
You can’t fault this on spectacle, and you can’t fault Wayne on his rockingly good creation.
But the brilliance of the presentation cannot conceal the thinness of the content.

cn.t: Jeff Wayne's musical adaptation struggles to translate from album to stage, with critics finding it bombastic but dramatically inert, relying heavily on spectacle over substance despite impressive production values.
